messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 72

He is a 46-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life trying to become someone who writes clean code, keeps deadlines, pays the mortgage on time, and drives home each evening to his wife. From the outside, his life now looks orderly and highly structured, the life of a successful software engineer. What emerges over several sessions, though, is how much of that order has been built in opposition to a much earlier world shaped by combat.

He is in his early twenties when he is conscripted during a period of armed conflict in his home country. At first he tells this part of his story flatly, almost as if he is reciting facts from someone else’s biography. He says he learns quickly not to ask questions. Days are organized around movement, waiting, and the constant possibility of attack. He remembers the heat most vividly, then the smell—wet earth, sweat, metal, blood. The event he returns to again and again happens during a patrol near a rural village. There is gunfire from a direction they do not expect. Men around him drop to the ground, shouting. He sees one of the soldiers he has eaten with for months struck in the neck. He tries to drag him, feels his body resist, hears screaming that he later realizes is his own. Mortar fire follows. He remembers dirt hitting his face, the sense that the air itself is exploding. At one point he lies still beneath brush and dead leaves, certain that if he breathes too loudly he will be found and killed. By the time the firing stops, several men are dead. He survives, but he says that from that day onward something in him “stays there.”

After the war, he leaves the country, studies, and builds a new life with determination that sounds almost punishing. He becomes skilled with computers because the logic feels safe. In programming, problems have causes, patterns, and solutions. If he is careful enough, he can prevent disaster. He marries, finds stable work, and gains a reputation for being meticulous. Coworkers know him as quiet, dependable, and unusually calm in technical emergencies. They do not see that when servers go down unexpectedly and alarms start sounding in the office, his body reacts before his mind does. His chest tightens, his shoulders lock, and for a split second he is back in that village, scanning for where the threat is coming from.

At home his wife has learned that certain things change him instantly. Fireworks send him inside before the first burst has faded. Helicopters make him stop speaking midsentence. If a car backfires near a crosswalk, he drops his keys or crouches reflexively, then looks around with embarrassed fury. At night he sleeps lightly and in fragments. He says he does not really sleep so much as “wait for morning.” When the nightmares come, they are intensely sensory. He wakes drenched, heart pounding, convinced for several moments that he smells smoke and mud. Sometimes he shouts in a language he rarely uses anymore. His wife used to try to wake him quickly, but once he swung an arm so hard that he nearly hit her, and now she waits at a distance until he recognizes the room.

He avoids war movies, crowded festivals, and conversations about military service. For years he tells himself this is preference, not fear. But the world has gradually narrowed. He chooses routes with less traffic, sits facing entrances in restaurants, and becomes agitated if his back is exposed. He checks locks repeatedly before bed. In the office, he prefers noise-canceling headphones not only for concentration but because sudden sounds feel intolerable. Even there, he is always monitoring: who is entering, what that sound was, whether the stairwell door just slammed.

He carries a persistent guilt that does not soften under logic. He speaks of the soldier who died while he was trying to drag him and wonders, with a painful circularity, whether he let go too soon, whether he should have gone back, whether surviving meant he failed some test of loyalty. When he sees news footage of conflict or displaced families, he becomes withdrawn for days. His wife says he grows distant in a way that feels like watching him leave the room while still sitting in front of her.

Over time, his irritability has become harder for him to contain. Small disruptions—a software bug introduced by a junior developer, a dish breaking in the kitchen, an unexpected knock at the door—can trigger an outsized surge of anger. He hates this about himself. He is especially ashamed that his body reacts to his family as if danger lives there too. He wants closeness but often feels emotionally numb, as though tenderness requires access to a part of himself that has long been sealed off for survival.

What he describes in the present is not only memory, but a life organized around trying not to remember. He has built competence, discipline, and safety around himself, yet the battlefield remains active inside him. Even now, decades later, he lives as though the next attack could come at any moment.
